node.label: Jan de Vries
node.date_label: The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis, 1600–1750 1976 · “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” 1994 · with van der Woude, The First Modern Economy 1997 · The Industrious Revolution 2008
node.description: An economic historian of the Netherlands and early modern Europe at Berkeley. The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis (1976) studied “the last great epoch before the onset of industrialization”; Pomeranz later called it “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”. His “industrious revolution”, proposed in his Economic History Association presidential address published in 1994, was meant “to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting”: “a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon”. In The Industrious Revolution (2008) he dated it to “roughly 1650–1850”, when households in north-western Europe and British North America reallocated “the time of their members” to earn money and to buy goods. He took the term from Akira Hayami, who had contrasted Japan’s labour-intensive path with Western industrialisation. He built the argument on the revisionist macroeconomics that cut British growth estimates “by more than half”, on the Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, and on Becker’s household economics; against a supply-side orthodoxy he illustrated with Mokyr, he sought to “restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (2008). With Ad van der Woude he presented the Dutch Republic as “the first modern economy” (1997), against historians who saw its achievement as “backward looking”; van Zanden doubted that Dutch growth was much faster than England’s (2002). Pomeranz used the industrious revolution for Chinese households (2000). Reviewers found The Industrious Revolution “on all the main points, convincing” (Voth, 2009), or thought it made consumption a new “deus ex machina” and played down power between the sexes (van Nederveen Meerkerk, 2009). From the history of papermaking, Leonard Rosenband challenged its chronology and mechanism: paperworkers already laboured long hours at the outset of the period, and women and adolescents worked for wages in paper mills long before it (2016).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Jan de Vries; The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis, 1600–1750 (1976); “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (Journal of Economic History, 1994); with Ad van der Woude, The First Modern Economy: Success, Failure, and Perseverance of the Dutch Economy, 1500–1815 (1997); The Industrious Revolution: Consumer Behavior and the Household Economy, 1650 to the Present (2008). Readers and critics: Kenneth Pomeranz (2000); Philip Huang (2002); Jan Luiten van Zanden (2002); Hans-Joachim Voth and Elise van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Leonard Rosenband (2016).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-18: the 1976 book’s chapter 1 opening and contents on Cambridge Core; the 1994 article’s abstract and reference list on Cambridge Core; Cambridge University Press excerpts of The First Modern Economy (1997, chapter 1, pp. 1–5, OCRed) and The Industrious Revolution (2008, chapter 1, pp. 1–10); Voth’s and van Nederveen Meerkerk’s reviews (2009) in full; van Zanden (2002) and Rosenband (2016) in abstract. Pages of the 1994 article were read in earlier revisions and support existing strands and edges; this entry quotes the article only from its publisher abstract. The rest of each book is unread, including the 2008 book’s chapters on hours of work, consumption and the breadwinner household, which are known only as Voth reports them. The First Modern Economy is co-authored with van der Woude. His essay on Pomeranz in the Historically Speaking forum of 2011 is known only through Peer Vries and is not used. The household mechanism stays on consumption/household_labor and economic/household_demand; whether it explains industrialisation is argued in the debate entry capitalismdebates.

proposed_edges.relationship: The “industrious revolution” applied to Chinese household labour (2000), and de Vries’s 1976 book cited as “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000; later-edition preview, read): labour deployment in Chinese families “seems to closely resemble the reorientation of labor, leisure, and consumption toward the market that Jan DeVries has called Europe’s ‘industrious revolution’” (p. 17; n. 28 cites DeVries 1994b); the contents list a section “Family Labor in China and Europe: ‘Involution’ and the ‘Industrious Revolution’”; “A good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis is DeVries 1976” (p. 3 n. 2). Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 520–521, read in revision 1.144) reads the borrowing critically: “it is surprising that Pomeranz would have tried to equate the Yangzi delta with de Vries’ industrious revolution”, “along the same lines as R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”; “he tries to take the revolution out of de Vries’ industrious revolution.” The use is Pomeranz’s; de Vries’s own later judgement of The Great Divergence (Historically Speaking, 2011) is unread and not drawn. The Huang–Pomeranz dispute over involution is on edges 1043–1044.

proposed_edges.relationship: With van der Woude, the Dutch Republic as “the first modern economy”, 1500–1815, against readings of its achievement as “backward looking”, joining Annales structural history to the New Economic History (1997); van Zanden doubted that Dutch growth was much faster than England’s (2002)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: De Vries and van der Woude, The First Modern Economy (1997, chapter 1, pp. 1–5 read in the publisher excerpt, OCRed): historians including Hobsbawm, Braudel and Wallerstein “felt certain that the Dutch achievement was essentially backward looking, the culmination of something with no future” (p. 1); they quote North and Thomas, for whom the Netherlands was “the first country to achieve sustained economic growth” (p. 2); “With this work we accept the challenge of the modern historical schools; indeed, we even seek to integrate them”: the Annales school, which “advocated a break with ‘event-centered history’”, and cliometrics, which “shifted the focus of the literature from politics and institutions to markets and rational decision makers” (p. 4); “This book, in short, presents the history of the first modern economy” (p. 4). Van Zanden (EHR 2002, abstract, read): “economic growth in the Netherlands was probably not much faster than in England, as is clear from the development of real wages”, and its modernity “appears to be a product of economic and institutional changes in the middle ages.” The book’s sectoral and analytical chapters are unread; the claim is the co-authors’ framing. De Vries’s criticism of the “backward looking” reading is recorded here, not as arrows to Braudel or Hobsbawm, because one paragraph groups them with Barbour and Wallerstein.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, with Hajnal’s marriage pattern, as one of the literatures that “guided my thinking” (2008)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, p. 8, publisher excerpt, read): among four “modern developments in history and economics” that “have guided my thinking”, “3. The Western European Marriage Pattern. The pioneering work of ‘The Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure’ established the view that the nuclear family structures of modern western European countries and their offshoots are not a product of industrialization but have much earlier origins”, with “the seminal articles of John Hajnal”; “its distinctive economic behavior remains an open question.” The 1994 article’s reference list (Cambridge Core, metadata) cites Wrigley and Schofield (1981), Laslett (1965, 1977) and Hajnal (1965). The influence is credited to the Cambridge Group and Hajnal, not to Wrigley alone; demography/john_hajnal already records Hajnal as a resource for de Vries.

proposed_edges.relationship: Demand restored against the supply-side orthodoxy, which de Vries illustrates with Mokyr’s view that the Industrial Revolution’s “when,” “where” and “how fast” are “to be sought first and foremost in supply” (1977; 2008)
proposed_edges.map_label: De Vries restores demand, citing Mokyr (2008)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, pp. 6–7, publisher excerpt, read): “Studies of modern economic growth are inevitably founded on a decisive ‘supply-side’ advance”; Adam Smith left no doubt that “The consumer responds to the developing productive forces, not the other way around”, with n. 17 quoting Mokyr’s “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” (JEH 1977, p. 1005): “The determination of ‘when,’ ‘where,’ and ‘how fast’ are to be sought first and foremost in supply, not demand-related processes”; “What began as an effort to restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (p. 7). Mokyr’s 1977 abstract (Cambridge Core, read): demand factors “were definitely of a secondary order of importance”. The 1994 article’s reference list cites the 1977 article. Qualification: de Vries cites Mokyr as an exemplar of a general orthodoxy; this is not a reply to a Mokyr text on the industrious revolution, and no reply by Mokyr was read.
